title: Distributed systems depth: consensus, replication and failure
goal: Go beyond box-and-arrow diagrams: understand how replicated systems agree, fail and recover by reading the key papers and implementing a replicated store yourself.

steps.title: MIT 6.5840 (6.824) Distributed Systems
steps.note: Lectures, readings and the famous Raft and key-value labs. Do the labs; reading alone is not enough.

steps.title: The Raft consensus algorithm
steps.note: The paper, an interactive visualisation and implementations to compare against.

steps.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
steps.note: Quorums, vector clocks, sloppy quorums and anti-entropy in one readable paper.

steps.title: Glossary: consensus, quorum, split brain, fencing token
steps.note: Search these terms and follow the related links.

steps.title: A replicated key-value store that survives failures
steps.brief: Implement a leader-based replicated store (the MIT labs are a good scaffold). Add a test harness that kills nodes, delays and drops messages, and checks that acknowledged writes are never lost and reads are linearizable where you promise it.
steps.deliverable: A repository with the store, a fault-injection test suite and a short document explaining which guarantees you provide and which you do not.

steps.title: Consensus, coordination, microservice patterns, search and security modules
steps.note: SD modules 11 to 16 are not written on this site yet. The papers and course above cover the same ground in the meantime.

exit: You can explain how Raft elects a leader and why a committed entry cannot be lost.
You can say what CAP and PACELC predict for a given store and what that means for a feature you are designing.
Your fault-injection tests find at least one real bug in your own implementation, which you fix.
